newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German economic picture mixed ahead of EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German economic picture mixed ahead of EMU.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Thursday presented a vision of long-term low inflation in Germany, stretching right up to 1999, when the German mark will be merged into the single European currency.
But it warned that Germany was heading toward monetary union with its economy far from problem-free, with joblessness and public budget deficits still high.

In its January monthly report, the central bank said it expected inflation to stay below two percent for the next two years, with prices capped by high unemployment, globalisation of markets and the the general view that inflation is an evil.
"For a variety of reasons such a scenario seems entirely realistic for the next two years, throughout the remaining period of existence of the mark," the central bank said.

But two sets of data released on Friday served as a reminder that low inflation -- even if it lays the basis for growth -- can also be a sign of weak demand in the economy, which in turn may prevent growth from gaining pace.
German retail sales data for November and the wholesale price index for December released on Thursday continued to give a subdued picture for consumer demand in Germany.
The Federal Statistics Office in Wiesbaden said that retail sales were down by a real two percent on a year-on-year basis in November, despite the introduction of longer shop hours.
Seasonally adjusted retail sales rose by two percent from October, but not enough to reverse a weak trend for the year, with sales down by one percent in the first 11 months of 1996.

Meanwhile, wholesale price data for December showed a rise of 0.3 percent month-on-month, while prices rose by 0.5 percent compared to December 1995. Averaging out the months of 1996, wholesale prices were down 0.6 percent on the previous year.

Furthermore, one Bundesbank council member, Hans-Juergen Krupp, even held out the prospect of a further interest rate cut to help alleviate joblessness, saying this sign of economic weakness was a problem the Bundesbank could not simply ignore.

In its report, the Bundesbank also pointed to a further sign of ill-health in the German economy -- the budget deficits and public borrowing which have remained high despite several years of efforts to rein in spending.

In a sign of the seriousness with which Bonn was viewing the problem, coalition sources said on Thursday German Finance Minister Theo Waigel would slap a freeze on extra government spending this month, but gave no date for its start.

The Bundesbank said the federal German government's cash position slipped further into the red in November -- growing to 15.4 billion marks ($9.66 billion) from 12 billion a year ago -- as traditional payments of "Christmas money" climbed from the year before.
That pushed the federal cash deficit for the year through November to nearly 84 billion marks, up from 38.39 billion marks during the same period a year earlier.

Germany's budgets are bathed in an unforgiving spotlight this year, with considerable effort needed if Bonn is to rein in spending to meet the budgetary targets for entry to a single currency. It overshot the goal in both 1995 and 1996.

In its report, the Bundesbank, which has often been criticised for an anti-single currency attitude, made clear that it was doing its bit to make the transition to Economic and Monetary Union as smooth as possible.

The powerful German central bank, which already effectively sets the pace for interest rates in Europe, deliberately broke with tradition in December to set a two-year orientation path for its main money policy indicator M3 money supply.
The move was aimed at giving Europe taste of its policy strategy right up to 1999, when responsibility for monetary policy will be taken over by the European central bank.
It set an expansion corridor of 3-1/2 to 6-1/2 percent for 1997, based on a central growth rate of five percent, and said it also expected M3 to grow by five percent on average in 1998.

In its report, the Bundesbank said the two-year orientation path would allow European central banks to coordinate their policies more smoothly over the next two years and meant the European Central Bank could tack its policy seamlessly onto the Bundesbank's stability course.
